title: Analysis: India’s power-sector emissions flat for two years due to clean-energy surge
text:
India’s power sector kept emissions flat for two years even as demand rose, showing that solar and other clean power can now absorb incremental load, but new coal capacity still raises system costs through lower utilization hours; the policy implication is that power governance must go beyond capacity expansion to curb marginal coal generation while tackling rising emissions from steel, cement, and other hard-to-abate sectors.

The piece uses the latest first-half-2026 data to test whether India’s clean-power expansion has moved from filling incremental demand to reshaping the system. It also speaks to the rebalancing between energy security and emissions reduction.

It sits at the intersection of India’s power planning, new coal approvals, and future NDC implementation.

title: Analysis: ‘Super El Niño’ reaches ‘remarkable’ all-time record
text:
The current El Niño is approaching historic extremes, showing how internal climate variability is stacking with long-term warming to amplify short-term shocks into cross-border pressures on food, energy, and disaster management; the article implies that El Niño should be treated not as background noise but as a trigger for contingency budgeting, forecasting systems, and cross-sector risk governance.

This matters now because the mid-September sea-surface record suggests the event is still intensifying, and strong El Niño episodes usually peak toward year-end. That creates a short window for disaster warning and fiscal preparedness.

It speaks to the seasonal calibration of national forecasting, food security, and disaster finance rather than a single negotiation track.

title: Climate Change and the Global South
source: Saleemul Huq and Hannah Reid · Climate Policy
text:
Huq and Reid reinsert climate change into the political economy of development. They argue that vulnerability in the Global South is produced not only by exposure to climate hazards, but also by poverty, weak infrastructure, agricultural dependence, limited fiscal capacity, and unequal historical responsibility. The article challenges approaches that narrow climate policy to emissions technology and insists that adaptation, poverty reduction, capacity building, and international support must be designed together. It helps readers evaluate climate finance and adaptation projects by asking whether they address the institutional roots of vulnerability rather than only the number of projects funded.

The article uses policy synthesis and vulnerability analysis. It is useful for framing development constraints, but it does not attempt single-variable causal identification.

Read alongside this issue’s “Nepal’s Gen Z Is Taking on the World’s Polluters Over Climate Disasters” to see how the Global South is re-linking loss and damage, adaptation, and responsibility.

How does vulnerability enter finance design? climate finance vulnerability adaptation distributional justice How does responsibility allocation shape compensation? loss and damage global south equity reparations

title: Producing the Climate: States, Scientists, and the Constitution of Global Governance Objects
text:
This article argues that climate is not a fixed governance object but something produced through interaction among state agencies, scientists, and international organizations, which shaped climate into a geophysical object. The author shows how the issue boundary shifts through co-production of state demand and scientific knowledge, as carbon sinks and land use entered the climate frame. Its value is to remind researchers that the dispute is not only how to govern climate, but what climate is defined to be.

The article combines science and technology studies with conceptual analysis of global governance, using historical process tracing of state-science interaction. It is an interpretive study rather than a single econometric model.

Read alongside Carbon Brief’s “Analysis: India’s power-sector emissions flat for two years due to clean-energy surge,” since it shows how power transition is reshaping the governance object itself, not just emissions outcomes.

How are climate objects redefined? governance objects science-policy climate politics co-production How do states shape scientific agendas? state-science relations epistemic communities climate knowledge policy framing

title: Factcheck: Reform UK’s 45 false or misleading claims about climate and energy
text:
Carbon Brief dismantles 45 misleading claims by Reform UK on climate science, net-zero, and energy prices, showing how the party blames deindustrialization and living-cost pressures on climate policy while sidestepping the IPCC consensus on human-caused warming and the institutional costs of scrapping targets, expanding fossil fuels, and rewriting renewables contracts.

The piece responds directly to the pre- and post-election move by right-populist actors in the UK to turn climate policy into a culture-war and cost-of-living issue, at a moment when the net-zero agenda is being redefined in electoral competition. Its value is to pull the debate back toward policy consequences.

It sits inside the UK’s domestic struggle over the net-zero target, energy contracts, and anti-net-zero mobilization.

title: Climate and the task for leaders at UNGA81
text:
E3G argues that leaders at UNGA81 must reframe climate action as a tool for security, affordability, stability, and growth rather than keeping it on a separate environmental track; the implication is that embedding the clean-energy transition in a broader crisis-management frame can sustain cross-issue coalitions and counter agenda fragmentation caused by geopolitical tension, economic pressure, and climate shocks.

This responds to the agenda window of UNGA81 and Climate Week NYC, using the high-level political gathering to restate the links among climate, development, energy, and security. It also shows advocates trying to seize leadership framing under conditions of layered crises.

It is positioned in the UNGA81 and Climate Week NYC high-level window, aimed at reinserting climate into leaders’ agendas.

title: El Niño: Indonesia fire emissions in 2026 ‘on track’ to match record for this century
text:
Carbon Brief shows that Indonesia’s fire emissions, driven by El Niño, are again approaching this century’s record, demonstrating that annual firefighting is insufficient for the structural risks of peatlands, land use, and transboundary haze; the article implies that fire response, land governance, emissions accounting, and regional cooperation need to be built into a longer-term forest-and-climate policy framework.

The piece matters now because the 2026 fire season is unfolding while the current El Niño is expected to last into 2027, implying that emissions and haze risks may persist. It links short-term disaster dynamics to medium-term policy design.

It sits at the intersection of Indonesia’s fire season and regional haze governance, while also affecting the global emissions and forest-governance agenda.

title: Between Mandate and Motivation
source: Mareike Well, Barbara Saerbeck, Helge Jörgens, Nina Kolleck · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The article shows that, despite a tightly constrained technocratic mandate, the UNFCCC Secretariat acts in an entrepreneurial style at agenda-initiation stage and remains cautiously entrepreneurial during policy formulation. Its core concern is not whether the Secretariat is “neutral,” but how international public administration can still shape multilateral climate outcomes by setting issues, facilitating bargaining, and sustaining ambition under strict mandate constraints.

The authors compare the Secretariat’s administrative styles and use negotiation-process analysis to derive ideal types.

Read alongside E3G’s UNGA81 agenda pieces in this issue, which similarly contest how international institutions define the boundaries of climate cooperation.

How do secretariats shape agenda formation under tight mandates? UNFCCC secretariat administrative style agenda setting international public administration How can constrained mandates still sustain policy ambition? technocratic mandate multilateral negotiations policy formulation entrepreneurial bureaucracy

title: Regional Governance of Global Climate Change: The North American Commission for Environmental Cooperation
source: Michele M. Betsill · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article evaluates the North American Commission for Environmental Cooperation (CEC) as a site of regional climate governance, arguing that the usual advantages of regional organizations—fewer actors, opportunities for issue linkage, and linkage between national and global governance systems—are limited in practice. It therefore insists that regional climate governance should not be treated as a natural supplement to global governance, but analyzed in terms of how it interacts with other mechanisms in a larger multilevel structure.

The article uses comparative institutional analysis of a regional body against three hypothesized advantages.

Read alongside this issue’s Carbon Brief piece on Indonesia fire emissions, because it shows that transboundary haze and regional coordination do not automatically yield effective governance.

When do regional institutions deliver effective climate governance? regional governance climate cooperation institutional design multilevel governance How is transboundary haze governed across borders? haze governance issue linkage regional institutions environmental cooperation

title: Analysis: UK solar power hits record high over summer 2026
text:
UK solar generation set a summer record under extreme heat and long daylight, showing that renewable deployment is beginning to turn climate stress into supply gains; the policy implication is that grid dispatch, storage, and interconnection rules must advance in parallel so weather-driven gains become system resilience rather than a short-lived output spike.

The piece responds to the 2026 summer when record heat, unusual sunshine, and record output coincided, showing that ‘more solar’ is no longer just an installation story but a governance problem of system adaptation to extremes. It shifts the debate from capacity growth to system integration.

It sits at the intersection of UK power-market reform and net-zero implementation, directly affecting the policy sequencing of interconnection, storage, and demand-side response.

title: How this summer’s heat and drought impacted crops in Europe – in six charts
text:
European agriculture is not facing a single weather shock but a compound risk in which heat, drought, and wildfires interact with energy prices, fertilizer supply, and fuel costs; the article’s mechanism is that output volatility has become an institutional vulnerability shaped by supply chains, input prices, and adaptation policy, requiring crop insurance, irrigation investment, fertilizer substitution, and food-price buffers to be governed together.

The article lands as governments begin assessing harvest losses, food-price pressure, and farm relief after the summer extremes. It moves short-term crop failures into Europe’s medium-term food-security and adaptation-finance agenda.

It sits at the intersection of EU agriculture and food-security policy, adaptation strategy, and the next round of loss-and-damage debates.

title: The state of the EU’s climate agenda: into autumn 2026 and beyond
text:
E3G places the EU climate agenda within a politics of independence and vulnerability, arguing that trade, technology, security, and extreme weather are pushing climate policy beyond a narrow emissions frame toward strategic resilience; the implication is that without aligning industrial policy, energy security, and climate goals, the EU will struggle to sustain coherence and implementation through the autumn window.

The commentary directly targets the EU’s autumn legislative and coordination period, responding to the way security and industrial pressures have crowded the climate agenda. Its timing is political rather than data-driven: the hierarchy of priorities has already shifted.

It sits at the intersection of the Commission’s ‘independence moment’ narrative, member-state priority competition, and the next phase of climate implementation.

title: Gatekeeping the Greenland ice sheet: climate change data and the “upstream” production of global governance objects
source: Lin Alexandra Mortensgaard · European Journal of International Relations
text:
The article develops ‘gatekeeping’ to show that global governance objects are shaped not at the point of published results, but upstream when data are scoped, extracted, and preliminarily analyzed. Through multi-sited ethnography of Greenland ice-core science, the author shows how states and scientific institutions control the flow and content of raw climate data and moves data sovereignty to the start of knowledge production.

The author uses multi-sited ethnography, combining participant observation and semi-structured interviews across Greenland, Germany, and Denmark, to trace ice-core science in practice.

Read alongside this issue’s Carbon Brief piece on UK solar’s record output: both show that energy and climate governance are shaped not only at the results stage, but by how data, infrastructure, and institutional thresholds are set upstream.

Who controls raw climate data in governance settings? data sovereignty climate science gatekeeping ethnography How does upstream knowledge production shape policy outcomes? knowledge production global governance institutional power climate data

title: Planning for resilience
text:
The European Commission’s forthcoming Climate Resilience and Risk Management Integrated Framework should treat heatwaves not merely as emergency management, but as a single governance problem linking power-system resilience, adaptation finance, and regulatory coordination; otherwise member states will deepen vulnerability through fragmented responses and miss a window for institutionalization.

The argument is timed to Europe’s autumn 2026 legislative agenda, so the policy window is already open. It responds to the recent extreme summer and tries to turn seasonal crisis into the next round of institutional design.

This is an advance intervention in the EU’s adaptation and energy-security agenda as it moves toward legislative drafting and closure.

title: Why the clean energy transition needs information integrity
text:
The clean energy transition is now constrained not only by technology and cost, but by information manipulation that reshapes public perceptions, amplifies political resistance, and weakens policy enforceability; information integrity must therefore be treated as part of energy governance through platform rules, communication design, and regulatory oversight.

The piece is timed to a period when the transition is accelerating and renewables are breaking records, shifting the question from whether transition is possible to how it can be sustained in a contested information environment. It also speaks directly to current pressures on policy communication and narrative control.

This is a governance-toolbox intervention aimed at the intersection of platform governance and climate-policy coordination.

title: Climate change exposes 580 million children to 20 extra ‘heat-stress days’ every year
text:
The study turns unequal exposure of children to humid heat stress from an abstract vulnerability into a measurable inequality, showing that high exposure in South Asia, Southeast Asia, and West Africa reflects not just climate risk but the interaction of demography, historical emissions, and uneven adaptation resources; climate justice and public-health finance must therefore enter heat-risk governance together.

The findings are framed against the 2026 European heatwaves and current global heat-risk debates, stressing that this is not a future projection but an already visible distributional pattern. The study provides a new evidence baseline for adaptation, health, and equity debates now underway.

This is an evidence input for the heat-adaptation and child-health agenda, suitable for insertion into UNFCCC adaptation discussions and public-health finance talks.

title: Global climate adaptation governance: Why is it not legally binding?
source: Nina Hall, Åsa Persson · European Journal of International Relations
text:
The article explains why adaptation governance under the UN climate framework remains low in precision and obligation: adaptation is treated as a contested global public good and is often bundled with mitigation commitments, producing many rules but limited legalization. Its contribution is to recast adaptation governance not as absent but as present with weak constraint, and to show that this weakness is itself the product of political compromise.

The article examines the precision and obligation of adaptation-related decisions through analysis of primary UNFCCC documents, secondary literature, expert and negotiator interviews, and participant observation at climate negotiations.

Read alongside E3G’s "Planning for resilience": both ask how adaptation moves from ad hoc response into institutionalized governance.

Why does adaptation remain weakly legalized? adaptation governance legalization UNFCCC global public goods How do package deals shape adaptation commitments? mitigation adaptation bargaining international climate negotiations

title: Conceptualizing Climate Governance Beyond the International Regime
source: Chukwumerije Okereke, Harriet Bulkeley, Heike Schroeder · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article argues that climate governance cannot be understood only through the lens of the international regime; subnational, private-sector, and cross-level actors must be included because climate policy is assembled through polycentric, multi-level governance. It emphasizes power, public-private authority relations, and the interaction of governing rationalities and practices.

The article uses conceptual review and theoretical synthesis, combining neo-Gramscian and governmentality perspectives to rebuild the analytical frame for climate governance.

Read alongside Inside Climate News’ "Will a Data Center Join the Philadelphia Bellwether District’s Mix of Manufacturers and Warehouses?": industrial redevelopment, data-center siting, and local energy governance all exemplify polycentric climate governance.

How does polycentric climate governance distribute power? polycentric governance climate governance public-private authority multi-level How does private authority enter climate policy? private authority governmentality climate policy global governance

title: How climate finance can deliver in a multipolar world
text:
E3G argues that amid geopolitical fragmentation, high interest rates, and shrinking development assistance, climate finance must shift from simple capital mobilization to a package centered on multilateral development banks, debt instruments, and risk-sharing mechanisms, or developing countries will be priced out of the transition.

The piece responds to a moment when multilateral cooperation is weakening as fiscal space tightens. It moves climate finance from a general commitment to the operational question of delivery in a fragmented world.

It sits at the intersection of climate finance, debt sustainability, and development finance, with direct implications for MDB reform and pre-COP mobilization arrangements.

title: Q&A: What is ‘long-duration energy storage’ – and why does the UK need it?
text:
Carbon Brief frames long-duration energy storage as the infrastructure that allows the UK to move from hour-by-hour balancing toward day-to-week flexibility in a wind-and-solar system, while Ofgem’s cap-and-floor scheme turns underpriced system flexibility into a financeable asset that can lower system costs and reduce curtailment risk.

The Q&A comes just as Ofgem has identified 16 projects for potential support, showing that storage has moved from concept to regulatory selection. It shifts the discussion from technology primer to regulatory design and investment incentives.

It sits within UK electricity-market reform, system-flexibility allocation, and the investment framework for net-zero infrastructure.

title: Inter-organizational Relations and Policy Coordination
source: Adam Kamradt-Scott · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The article focuses on policy coordination among international organizations and argues that, as member states face proliferating IOs, encouraging institutional collaboration has become a common governance response to reduce competition, conflict, and overlap. It also contends that ‘policy coordination’ remains underconceptualized in the literature and examines the Quadripartite’s efforts on antimicrobial resistance through national action plan adoption.

The article combines conceptual discussion with a case analysis of the Quadripartite’s coordination efforts, evaluating the diffusion of member states’ national action plans.

Read alongside E3G’s “How climate finance can deliver in a multipolar world” to see how multilateral coordination can be turned into workable financing and governance arrangements in a fragmented setting.

How does coordination become implementation? policy coordination international organizations implementation governance diffusion Which division of labor best reduces overlap? inter-organizational relations mandate overlap institutional collaboration multilateralism coordination
